253.title: Christianity: the two commandments
253.hook: Jesus names the greatest commandments: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40)
253.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the two great commandments, and some churches read them aloud in worship; Christians across traditions treat love of God and neighbor as the heart of the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pesach, the freedom meal. Your line was we were slaves, now free. Did you tell a story of freedom out loud? Day two hundred fifty-three, and a new visit: Christianity.

Imagine someone hands you a rulebook six hundred pages long and says: sum it up. One sentence. Most of us would panic, or pick something random, or cheat and say be good. In the Gospel of Matthew, a lawyer tries this on Jesus. It's a test, the text says, and a hard one: Jewish tradition counts six hundred and thirteen commandments in the Torah. Which one is the greatest? Jesus doesn't pick one. He picks two, and he picks them from the very scripture we spent last week visiting. Today we start our week with Christianity.
screen: `SUM IT UP IN ONE SENTENCE.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE GREATEST?` → `HE PICKS TWO.`

segments.voice: Here is his answer in the King James Version, Matthew twenty-two: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." If the first sounds familiar, it should. It comes from Deuteronomy, right beside the Shema we heard a week ago: hear, O Israel. The second comes from Leviticus, chapter nineteen. Jesus, a Jewish teacher, is quoting the Torah, and Christians have treated his pairing ever since as the center of their faith. Notice three things. First, the order: God first, neighbor second, but the second is like unto it, the same kind of thing. Many Christians say you can't really keep one without the other; a later letter in the New Testament says that someone who claims to love God and hates a brother is not telling the truth. Second, the word hang. Everything else hangs on these two, like a door on its hinges. Third, the small phrase as thyself. It assumes you already know how you want to be treated, and asks you to aim that at someone else. In Luke's Gospel, when a lawyer asks the follow-up question, and who is my neighbor, Jesus answers with a story, the good Samaritan, in which the neighbor turns out to be the stranger no one expected.
screen: `LOVE GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR AS YOURSELF.` · `ALL THE LAW HANGS ON THESE TWO.` · `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one neighbor to love concretely. Sit and let faces come. The person next door. The coworker who seems tired. The stranger who serves your coffee. Pick one. Then ask the as-yourself question: if I were them today, what small thing would I be glad of? A hand with the bins, a real hello, a message. Let the answer be small and doable. The bell holds the time.
Christianity, at its center: two commandments, love God and love your neighbor as yourself, on which all the law and the prophets hang. Today's word.
Your line: love your neighbor. Today, do the small thing you pictured for the neighbor you picked, before evening. Day two hundred fifty-three.

254.title: Christianity: blessed are
254.hook: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers (Matthew 5:3–9)
254.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize the Beatitudes, and churches read them often, especially on All Saints' Day; some use them as a daily examination of how they are living.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the two commandments, love God and love your neighbor as yourself. Your line was love your neighbor. Which neighbor got the small thing? Day two hundred fifty-four.

Scroll through any feed for a minute and you'll see who the world calls blessed. The rich. The winners. The ones on the beach with the perfect caption. Hashtag blessed. Now picture a hillside in Galilee, two thousand years ago. A crowd has followed a young teacher up the slope. He sits down, the way teachers did, and opens his mouth, and the first word out of it is blessed. Then he names who's blessed, and it's almost the opposite list. Today, in our week with Christianity: the Beatitudes, the opening of the Sermon on the Mount.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `A HILLSIDE IN GALILEE.` → `ALMOST THE OPPOSITE LIST.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter five. In the King James words: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Then those who mourn, who will be comforted. "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth." Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness. "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." The pure in heart, who shall see God. And then today's line: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The word behind blessed is Greek, makarios. It can mean happy, fortunate, well off, the kind of word you'd use for someone whose life has turned out right. So Jesus is saying: the people who are truly well off are the grieving, the gentle, the merciful, the ones making peace. Each line has two halves: who, and what's coming to them. Many Christians read the second halves as promises about God's kingdom, partly now and fully later. Two small things people often miss. Luke's Gospel has a shorter version, set on a level place, that says simply blessed be ye poor, and adds a set of woes. Christians have read Matthew's poor in spirit and Luke's poor side by side for centuries, and they disagree about how much to stress each. And notice the word in today's line: not peace-lovers, peacemakers. Making is work. It's the person who steps into the argument at the family dinner, or sends the first message after the fight. Jesus says they'll be called children of God.
screen: `THE POOR IN SPIRIT, THE MEEK, THE MERCIFUL.` · `MAKARIOS — HAPPY, WELL OFF.` · `WHO, AND WHAT'S COMING TO THEM.` · `NOT PEACE-LOVERS: PEACEMAKERS.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace once today. Sit, and bring to mind one small tension. A sharp text you haven't answered. A cold silence at home. Two friends not speaking. Don't solve it yet. Just picture the first peacemaking step: a softer word, a question instead of a point, an apology for your part. Breathe while you hold it. The bell holds the time.
Christianity, through the Beatitudes: blessed, makarios, truly well off, said of the meek, the merciful and the peacemakers. Today's word.
Your line: blessed are the peacemakers. Today, take the first peacemaking step you pictured, one softer word into one tense place. Day two hundred fifty-four.

255.title: Christianity: the Lord's Prayer
255.hook: the prayer Jesus taught his followers (Matthew 6:9–13)
255.howItsDone: Christians of every major tradition pray the Lord's Prayer, often daily, and congregations say it together in most services; Catholics call it the Our Father and pray it in the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Beatitudes. Your line was blessed are the peacemakers. Did one softer word go into one tense place? Day two hundred fifty-five.

There's a good chance you know some of this prayer even if you've never been to church. You've heard it at a funeral, or a school assembly, or a wedding, or in a film just before something goes badly wrong. Our Father, who art in heaven. Somewhere around two billion Christians share it: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, in hundreds of languages. It's probably the most widely prayed text on earth. And it began with a simple request. In Luke's Gospel, the disciples watch Jesus pray and ask him: teach us. Today: the prayer he gave them.
screen: `A FUNERAL, A SCHOOL, A FILM.` → `TWO BILLION VOICES.` → `TEACH US.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter six, in the King James Version: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread." Then forgiveness, as we forgive others; then protection from temptation and evil. It's short on purpose. Just before it, Jesus warns against heaping up words, as if length impressed God. Look at the shape. The first half faces God: the name, the kingdom, the will. The second half faces us: bread, forgiveness, protection. Big things, then small things, and the small things are allowed in the same breath. Now today's line. Daily bread. It sounds simple, but the Greek word translated daily, epiousios, appears almost nowhere else in all of Greek writing, and nobody is certain what it means. Daily? For tomorrow? Needed for existence? Early Christian writers already argued about it, and some read it as the bread of the Eucharist too. What everyone agrees on is the size of the request: enough for today. Not a year's supply. It echoes the manna in the wilderness, from the story of the going out from Egypt: bread that came each morning, enough for that day, and spoiled if hoarded. Christians pray it in different forms. Many Protestants end with for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. That line isn't in Luke or in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew, and at Catholic Mass it comes a little later, after another short prayer.
screen: `TEACH US TO PRAY.` · `GOD'S NAME FIRST, THEN OUR BREAD.` · `EPIOUSIOS — NOBODY IS SURE.` · `ENOUGH FOR TODAY, LIKE MANNA.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it slowly once. If you pray, you can pray it; if not, simply listen to it as words people have said for two thousand years. Our Father which art in heaven. Pause. Hallowed be thy name. Pause. Thy kingdom come. Give us this day our daily bread. Then sit with that one line. What is enough, just for today? The bell holds the time.
Christianity, through the Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught, God's name first, then bread for today. Today's word.
Your line: daily bread. Today, at one meal, notice that it's enough, and let tomorrow's worries wait until tomorrow. Day two hundred fifty-five.

256.title: Christianity: grace
256.hook: Christians speak of grace, God's love given before anything is earned
256.howItsDone: Many Christians say grace before meals, and churches speak of grace in preaching, baptism and communion; Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians each describe how grace works in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Lord's Prayer. Your line was daily bread, enough for today. Did one meal feel like enough? Day two hundred fifty-six.

Someone pays for your coffee. The person behind you in line, a stranger, and by the time you turn around they're gone. What's your first feeling? For a lot of us it isn't simple joy. It's a small itch. I should pay them back. I should pay it forward. I owe someone now. We are very good at keeping score, and very bad at receiving something we didn't earn. That itch is exactly where one of the biggest words in Christianity lands. Today: grace.
screen: `A STRANGER PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `THE ITCH: I OWE SOMEONE.` → `GRACE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament word is charis. In ordinary Greek it meant a favor, a gift, a kindness freely done, and the gratitude that answers it. Our words charity and charisma grow from the same family; so does eucharist, thanksgiving, which is coming up next week. Paul made charis the center of his letters. Here's the line many Christians know best, from Ephesians, in the King James Version: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. The gift comes first. Another letter, 1 John, puts it in six words: "We love him, because he first loved us." The order matters. Christians say God doesn't wait for people to become good enough to be loved. The love comes first, and goodness grows in answer to it. Where Christians differ is in how grace and human response fit together. Martin Luther and the Protestant reformers stressed that people are made right with God by grace through faith alone, not by works. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also say grace comes first and can't be earned, and they speak of it working through the sacraments and through a person's free cooperation, growing over a lifetime. Those differences have been argued, sometimes bitterly, for five hundred years, and in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint statement saying they now share a basic understanding. There's a reason the hymn Amazing Grace, written by John Newton, a former slave-ship captain, is still sung everywhere: it's the song of someone who knew he hadn't earned it.
screen: `CHARIS — A GIFT FREELY GIVEN.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES: THE GIFT OF GOD.` · `HE FIRST LOVED US.` · `HOW GRACE AND RESPONSE FIT TOGETHER.` · then, large: `GIVEN, NOT EARNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive one kindness without deflecting. Sit, and remember a gift you were given that you didn't earn. A friend who stayed. A teacher who saw something in you. A second chance. Notice the urge to explain it away, or to pay it back right now. Let that urge go quiet for a moment. Just receive it. Breathe in, and let it land. The bell holds the time.
Grace. Charis in Greek: a gift freely given; for Christians, God's love that comes before anything is earned. Today's word.
Your line: given, not earned. Today, when someone does you a kindness, say thank you and stop there. No but, no I owe you. Day two hundred fifty-six.

257.title: Christianity: Easter
257.hook: Christians believe Jesus died on the cross and rose again, and their hope rests there
257.howItsDone: Christians keep Holy Week before Easter, remembering the Last Supper and the crucifixion on Good Friday, then celebrate the resurrection on Easter Sunday, often with a vigil or sunrise service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grace, charis, love that comes first. Your line was given, not earned. Did you take a kindness and simply say thank you? Day two hundred fifty-seven.

Very early on a Sunday morning, before the sun is properly up, a few women walk to a graveyard carrying spices. They're going to do the last thing you can do for someone you loved: care for the body. They've been worrying the whole way about something practical. The tomb was sealed with a heavy stone. Who's going to move it? When they arrive, the stone is already rolled away. Everything Christians hope for grows out of what they found, and didn't find, that morning. Today, in our week with Christianity: Easter.
screen: `EARLY SUNDAY, CARRYING SPICES.` → `WHO WILL MOVE THE STONE?` → `ALREADY ROLLED AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the Friday. Jesus was arrested in Jerusalem during Passover and crucified by the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for rebels and slaves, slow and public, meant to shame. His followers scattered. Then the Sunday. All four Gospels tell of the empty tomb, each a little differently: who went, how many angels, who they met. In Matthew, the angel tells the women, in the King James words: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." In John's Gospel, Mary Magdalene stays weeping by the tomb, thinks the man beside her is the gardener, and knows him only when he says her name. The earliest written account is even older than the Gospels: a letter from Paul, written about twenty years after, passing on what he'd received, that Christ died, was buried, "and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." Christians say this is the center of everything. Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, their faith is in vain. Easter is the oldest and greatest Christian feast. Here's the link to our last visit: in many languages Easter is called Pascha, from Pesach, because it happened at Passover. On Easter morning many Orthodox Christians greet each other, Christ is risen, and answer, he is risen indeed. Western and Orthodox churches often celebrate on different Sundays, because they calculate the date with different calendars. For Christians, the hope is not that death was avoided, but that it was gone through, and came out the other side as new life.
screen: `CRUCIFIED UNDER PONTIUS PILATE.` · `HE IS NOT HERE: HE IS RISEN.` · `MARY, AND HER NAME SPOKEN.` · `PASCHA, FROM PESACH.` · then, large: `NEW LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the idea of new life. Whatever you believe about that morning, let the picture stay: a heavy stone, already moved. Bring to mind one thing in your life that feels sealed shut. A habit, a grief, a relationship. Don't force it open. Just hold the question: what would new life look like here? The bell holds the time.
Christianity, through Easter: Jesus crucified and, Christians say, risen on the third day. Their hope rests there. Today's word.
Your line: new life. Today, look for one small sign of it: a green shoot through concrete, a friend on the mend, a first step after a long stall. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

258.title: Christianity: love is patient
258.hook: Paul's hymn to love: patient, kind, not envious (1 Corinthians 13, where the KJV says "charity")
258.howItsDone: 1 Corinthians 13 is read at many Christian weddings and funerals, and some Christians use its list, patient, kind, not envious, as a daily check on how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Easter, the stone already rolled away. Your line was new life. Did you spot one small sign of it? Day two hundred fifty-eight.

If you've been to a wedding, you've probably heard it. Someone's cousin walks to the front, unfolds a piece of paper, and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone nods. It's lovely. It fits on a card. But here's the surprise. The man who wrote it wasn't thinking about weddings at all. He was writing to a church that was falling apart: people suing each other, showing off, forming cliques, looking down on the ones with less. Today, in our week with Christianity: one of the most famous chapters on love ever written, and the fight it was written into.
screen: `A COUSIN READS AT A WEDDING.` → `IT WASN'T WRITTEN FOR WEDDINGS.` → `A CHURCH FALLING APART.`

segments.voice: The writer is Paul, and the church is in Corinth, a busy Greek port city. His first letter to them is full of their problems: rival factions, lawsuits, rich members eating well at the shared meal while poorer ones went hungry. And the Corinthians were proud of their spiritual gifts: speaking in tongues, prophecy, knowledge. So in chapter thirteen Paul says, in effect: without love, all of that is noise. Then he describes love, and the King James Version says it like this: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Why charity? The Greek word is agape, from the same family of words the Gospels use in the two commandments we met a few days ago, love God and love your neighbor. Latin translators rendered it caritas, and the King James translators followed with charity, which in 1611 meant a deep, self-giving love, not only giving money. Modern translations mostly say love. Suffereth long is today's line: love is patient. Now read it again, knowing it was written to people who were quarreling. It isn't a description of a feeling. It's a list of behaviors, almost a job description. Patient. Kind. Not envious. Not showing off. Not keeping score. Paul ends the chapter with a line many people know by heart: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Christians of every church read this chapter, at weddings and funerals, and many also read it as a picture of how God loves. For a church that was falling apart, the instructions were simple: be patient with each other first.
screen: `CORINTH: A CHURCH IN PIECES.` · `WITHOUT LOVE, ALL OF IT IS NOISE.` · `AGAPE, CARITAS, CHARITY.` · `NOT A FEELING: A LIST OF BEHAVIORS.` · then, large: `LOVE IS PATIENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient once today, starting here. Bring to mind the person who tries your patience most. The slow one, the loud one, the one who never replies. Picture the moment it usually snaps. Now picture the same moment, slowed down: one breath before you answer. Suffereth long. Rehearse that breath now, a few times. The bell holds the time.
Christianity, through Paul's hymn: agape, love that is patient and kind, written to a church in pieces. Today's word.
Your line: love is patient. Today, when the familiar snap comes, take the one breath first. Just once counts. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

259.title: Christmas, the child
259.hook: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus, God come as a child in a stable (Luke 2)
259.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Christmas with services on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, many after the four weeks of Advent; many churches set up a nativity scene and read Luke 2 aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Paul's hymn to a quarreling church. Your line was love is patient. Did you take the one breath before the snap? Day two hundred fifty-nine, the last day of our visit to Christianity.

Think of everything Christmas has collected over the centuries. Trees indoors. Lights on every roofline. A man in a red suit. Songs in every shop from November on. Now peel all of it away, layer by layer, until you get to what's underneath. It's small. A young couple far from home. Nowhere proper to stay. A baby, wrapped up tight and laid in an animal's feeding trough. And the first people told about it are shepherds, working the night shift. Today, to end our week with Christianity: Christmas, the child.
screen: `TREES, LIGHTS, A RED SUIT.` → `PEEL IT ALL AWAY.` → `A BABY IN A FEEDING TROUGH.`

segments.voice: Luke chapter two. Mary and Joseph travel to Bethlehem for a census. In the King James words: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. Then an angel appears to shepherds in the fields: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." Christians call this the incarnation: the belief that God, in Jesus, came into the world not as a king in a palace but as a helpless baby, among animals, announced first to laborers. Now the honest part. The Gospels never give a date; December twenty-fifth was chosen by the church centuries later, and many Orthodox churches celebrate on January seventh because they keep an older calendar. Luke doesn't mention snow, or cold, or a donkey, or how many animals were there. The word translated inn may simply mean a guest room in a crowded family house. The cold of our carry comes from carols and from how people have pictured it for centuries, not from the text. But the picture has lasted for a reason: a child in the cold is someone you can't ignore. Look back over our week. Two commandments: love your neighbor. The Beatitudes: blessed are the peacemakers. The Lord's Prayer: daily bread. Grace: given, not earned. Easter: new life. Paul: love is patient. And the child, whose birth all of it looks back to.
screen: `NO ROOM IN THE INN.` · `GOOD TIDINGS, TOLD TO SHEPHERDS.` · `GOD AS A HELPLESS BABY.` · `NO DATE, NO SNOW IN THE TEXT.` · then, large: `A CHILD IN THE COLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something small. Sit, and picture the scene without the decorations: the trough, the cold night, the shepherds. Then let the picture move to now. Who near you is, in some way, out in the cold? A new neighbor. A lonely relative. Someone sleeping outside. Choose one small gift you could give today: a coat, a meal, an hour. The bell holds the time.
Christmas: Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus, God come as a baby, laid in a manger because there was no room. Today's word.
Your line: a child in the cold. Today, give the small thing you chose, to someone out in the cold. Day two hundred fifty-nine. Tomorrow we visit the Catholic tradition.

fork.setup: you're an angel with the biggest news in the world. who do you tell first?
fork.reveal: in Luke 2 the angel appears to shepherds in the fields: good tidings of great joy, to all people.

original.note: Greek of Luke 2:7: manger, a feeding trough.

trapdoor: what you thought: presents, a tree and a red suit.
what it means: the feast of Jesus' birth: God, Christians say, come as a baby.
what a scholar hears: Luke's kataluma may mean guest room, not inn; the date of December 25 is attested only centuries later.
